Stay out of Excel Hell

​

Why Copying formulas is not the same with Microsoft Excel Tables and what to do about it!

If you have tried to copy a structured reference formula from one column to another, I am guessing you have noticed that it often does not change the column reference. This is because Microsoft Excel Tables and structured references behavior different than structured references.

​

If I enter the formula = A1*B1 in cell A2 and then copy it across the columns, it will look like the following:

​

Notice how every time I move over one column the formula moves with it. However with a table it depends on how you copy it on whether the references will change or not.

​

When copying data, four options exist:

  • You can copy and paste
  • You can copy right
  • You can use the fill handle
  • You can use the fill function from the menu bar

​

When working with tables, only the Fill handle will change the column reference in the formula when copying the formula from one cell to another. All others will continue referencing the original column referenced in the formula. In the below example, we summed month 1 from the table, and only the fill handle method resulted in the columns adjusting to months 2, 3, and 4 when we copied them across. This has frustrated many a person when using tables as formulas do not behave the same as they do with unstructured references.

​

Learning this will make it easier to work with tables, and given the many benefits of tables, they are worth working with.

Business Partner's Corner

​

Have you ever been in a month end or budget meeting where it feels like folks want to sleep, poke their eyes out, or run out of the room?

I’ve been in several meetings where I couldn’t wait for the meeting to END. I could feel the audience saying in their ‘inside voices’, let’s get through this and let’s go get our coffee refilled. The funny thing was that I was often leading the meeting 😊

Several years later and many experiences behind me I know there are proven ways to truly engage cross functional team and have an engaging, productive, and fun meeting.

​

LET’S MAKE FINANCE FUN!
​

Here are five ways to achieve that.

1) Use the BLUF principle (BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT). In simple terms, less is more. Let’s not get trapped into showing excruciating amounts of detail. Tell the story. Cut to the chase of what is important and what actions can be taken.

​

2) Use visuals to paint the picture. Nothing is worse than a deck full of numbers. Visuals are much more engaging and much easier to understand. Keep them simple and have one key message/takeaway per visual. Keep the detailed financials in the appendix!

​

3) Avoid financial jargon and acronyms. Nothing is worse than a person spewing acronyms to a nonfinancial audience. IRR, NPV, EBITDA, DIOH, DPO, etc. Keep it simple and explain your concepts in everyday English. My rule of thumb is to think of the person with the least financial knowledge in the room. They should understand what you’re talking about

​

4) Have some fun. My partner (Paul Barnhurst) and I have a ton of fun in our training sessions. It started accidently when I had a technical issue playing a video and asked him to tell a joke. He pulled out his ‘Excel joke book’ and the rest was history. We now tell jokes in every session and get smiles and awesome engagement (even if the jokes are terrible).

​

5) Set the tone with your energy and body language – building on the fun theme,

your energy, your voice, and body language will set the tone for the meeting. I recently took a fantastic public speaking course and learned that the audience will never have as much energy or fun as the person leading the meeting or giving the speech. Bring authentic and intentional energy to the meeting! If it is tough month end, you may want to skip the jokes, but you can still bring positive energy. What can we do to improve next month or next quarter? That is great business partnership.

​

Bonus tip: Keep the meetings short and sweet. Don’t go on and on. Get to the point and your audience will always appreciate time back. Often in meetings we use the whole time rather than being intentional and thoughtful on what we really want to get out of the meeting.

The FP&A Guy's Tech Tips

​

This week's tech tip is a brief summary of the 3rd Gen FP&A Market Guide released last week. One of the most important tools for FP&A professionals is planning software.

​

Download a copy of the guide today.

​

The guide highlighted 14 different tools, as seen in the chart below. The chart provides a way to segment the different tools across market size and integration with spreadsheets.

​

The market size is shown at the bottom of the chart. This consists of small, medium, and enterprise. It is important to remember that many of the tools listed in the guide serve more than one market, but the chart captures the primary market. Horizontally, we show the product types, which consist of six categories.

​

  • Spreadsheet Native - A spreadsheet native tool is a web app that relies on the spreadsheet as its primary calculation engine. Without the spreadsheet the tool would not be able to function on its own. Some examples include Cube, Datarails, Drivepoint, and Vena.

​

  • Web App - High Spreadsheet Integration - A tool with high spreadsheet integration means it is tightly integrated with either Excel or Google Sheets and is one step away from a spreadsheet native tool. Some examples include TM1, Power Excel, and Aleph.

​

  • Web App - Medium Spreadsheet Integration - These are tools that have their own calculation engines and spreadsheets but also strive to make it easy to work with spreadsheets such as Excel and Google Sheets. Some examples include Adaptive, Vareto, Mosaic, and Abacum.

​

  • Web App - Low Spreadsheet Integration - These tools have some basic spreadsheet integration but primarily focus on replacing your spreadsheet. Some examples include Forecastr and Runway.

​

  • Web App - Spreadsheet Replacement - These tools are focused on replacing your spreadsheet and have minimal integration with traditional spreadsheets. Some examples include Anaplan, Pigment, Farseer, and Drivetrain.

​

  • Planning App within BI Tool - These are tools that have built a planning application on top of a BI tool. Many of these applications have been built upon Qlik or Power BI. Some examples include Lumel, Acterys, Aimplan, Fiplana, and Power On.

Ron's Recommendations

​

The Presentation Secrets of Steve Jobs

How Finance individuals can be insanely great in front of any audience!

​

Steve Jobs was a legend in so many ways. One of those was that he was a phenomenal presenter, and this book captures the method behind his brilliant, captivating, and memorable presentations.

​

Consider an upcoming Finance presentation or conversation. It can be a month-end review, a budget presentation, a business review, or an investment analysis. What lessons can you learn from the one and only Steve Jobs?

​

Here is the three-part framework that Jobs used:

​

1) Create the story – Before updating the usual ‘deck’ or ‘template’, roll around in the data and find what you want to truly convey. Be deliberate with this step. What are the headlines? What are the top three conclusions (maximum) and what do you want your cross-functional partners to remember or take action on? Less is more and this is an important but hard lesson for detail-oriented individuals to learn. This step is important and often missed as we often jump into the detail.

​

2) Deliver the experience – This could be using effective and intentional visuals instead of heavy numbers charts. It could be using zippy or simple language instead of financial jargon. It could be getting your audience involved early and often in the presentation. I love the thought of Finance not falling into the stereotypical boring bean counter content. Let’s make it impactful, interesting, and insightful.

​

3) Refine and rehearse – Steve Jobs was famous for his practice sessions. Everything had to be perfect, and he drove those around him nuts. He was a perfectionist and every word mattered. This approach was a major reason that Apple presentations were legendary. Here is what we can do:

​

  • Practice with Finance colleagues. In one of my experiences, we set up a finance-only meeting the day before the Executive review. It was great to iron out any flaws and discuss contentious issues.
  • Body language & voice – practicing includes how you use your voice and body language. The energy the presenter has is so important for the audience so make it count with practice.

​

Finance can be fun and engaging if we focus on it and get a little better every time!

​

Who better to learn from then a master storyteller like Steve Jobs!
